sources.entry: CPU Isolation - Ties isolcpus, nohz_full, IRQ affinity, RCU offload and cpusets into one recipe, and lists the jitter it leaves.

summary.title: CPU Isolation
summary.one_liner: Learn how to dedicate a CPU to a workload by combining scheduler domain isolation, IRQ affinity, nohz_full, cpusets and boot parameters, and how to trace the remaining kernel noise.
keywords: reduce timer tick interrupts on isolated cpu
how to isolate a cpu for low latency
takeaways: Isolating a CPU means moving or shutting down kernel housekeeping work (unbound workqueues, kthreads, timers, IRQs, RCU callbacks) away from it.
Scheduler domain isolation uses cgroup v2 cpuset isolated partitions (CONFIG_CPUSETS=y) or isolcpus with the domain flag; cpusets are recommended because they are runtime-tunable.
nohz_full (CONFIG_NO_HZ_FULL=y) stops the tick on a CPU running a single task, but forbids kernel entry from that CPU and requires a stable clocksource; housekeeping CPUs run a 1Hz residual tick.
A worked example isolates CPU 7 of 8 using nohz_full=7, irqaffinity=0-6, isolcpus=managed_irq,7 and nosmt, then verifies with ftrace sched_switch and irq_vectors events.
Remaining jitter can come from page faults (use mlock), SMT siblings, cpufreq changes, deep C-states and firmware SMIs; rtla osnoise and dynticks-testing help analyze noise.
summary.summary: The kernel documentation page defines CPU isolation as keeping a CPU free of kernel noise from asynchronous events (interrupts, timers, workqueues, kthreads) and synchronous events (syscalls, page faults). It explains housekeeping work and covers isolation features in turn: scheduler domain isolation, IRQ isolation, and full dynticks (nohz_full), each with requirements, constraints and tradeoffs. A full example isolates CPU 7 via kernel boot parameters and a cgroup v2 cpuset, runs a userspace loop, and traces sched_switch and IRQ vector events with ftrace. It closes with a checklist of other jitter sources and debugging tools such as rtla-osnoise and dynticks-testing.
